newsitem.title: BOSNIA: FEATURE - Bosnia's crippled giant refuses to go quietly.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bosnia's crippled giant refuses to go quietly.

text.p: What was once Bosnia's most prestigious and competitive company emerged shattered from a devastating 3-1/2 year war.
But Energoinvest is not yet ready to give up the fight for its share of the market.

Founded in 1951 in communist-ruled Yugoslavia by an engineer with a vision, it brought together five core businesses-- production of electrical power equipment, technological process equipment, computers and automation, non-ferrous metals and gas, oil and chemistry.
The company's market-oriented business approach bore fruit. In 1990, the last year it published results before the war, Energoinvest made $1.7 billion in total sales and employed 45,000 people.
But Yugoslavia's bloody disintegration tore Energoinvest apart just as it did Yugoslavia's six republics.

Energoinvest factories and divisions were seized by newly formed states, who imposed state ownership on the company that previously operated under social ownership -- employees were shareholders but could not sell their shares.
The company now controls only 10 percent of its pre-war facilities.

"Because of the violent behaviour of the authorities, all of them -- Serb, Croat and Bosniac (Moslem), we control only 10 percent of our capacity, mainly in the Sarajevo region," Bozidar Matic, a member of the board of directors, told Reuters.
"They may have taken the machines and walls, but the brain -- researchers, engineers, strategists and managers -- is still intact and we have a come-back strategy," Matic said
COMPANY NEEDS $30 MILLION FOR A FACTORY

The company's engineers worked in cellars during the 1992-1995 Bosnian war and managed to develop an advanced model of a circuit breaker used in high-voltage equipment, a sector in which it held an esteemed fifth position in the world.
The product, tested and approved by Italian and Dutch laboratories last year, could bring Energoinvest back to foreign markets. But Matic said it needs a $30 million injection to build a factory.

"With a $15 million investment, somebody could get a 50-50 partnership. To be a partner in the production of such high technology for such a small amount of money, you can only have it in a country like this," he said.
In a politically volatile country where the presence of NATO peacekeepers prevents a return to war, only a small number of foreign investors dare to tread in Bosnia.
"This is no worse than investing in one of the Latin American countries," Matic argues. "Just consider it a junk-bond investment."
REASSURING INVESTORS
But much more needs to be done to reassure investors. Politicians are still debating privatisation proposals and the government has yet to adopt free-market reforms.

About 10 percent of Energoinvst was privatised with economic reforms that began in former Yugoslavia in 1989 and, if it had not been for war, the company would have gone public with about 50 percent of its capital.
It will insist on preserving Energoinest's trade-mark name when privatised and plans to eliminate less promising divisions, Matic said.

Energoinvest hopes investors will also consider the company's experience in building transmission lines. One of its two pre-war factories is in Sarajevo and is fully equipped but needs marketing support, Matic said.
"We need a strong guarantor because our banks are too weak. Our facilities are fine, we just need the market-presentation support from an investor."
The war halted negotiations with British conglomerate Lonrho, which was interested in strategic investment in transmission lines.
Energoinvest is eagerly awaiting privatisation legislation to clear the way for foreign investment, Matic says.
"Until our ownership issue is resolved by privatisation, investors do not want an equal joint venture with us and ask for a majority control," he said.
"We are now like an AIDS-infected patient only we don't have AIDS but a disease called presence of state in the company.
"But we are not giving up because the brain that made the company is still here and we shall build it again with new knowledge."
